Yes, the Constitutionality of the 19th Amendment was challenged in the Supreme Court, in 1922's Leser v. Garnett.

Oscar Leser attempted to have two women's names struck from the Maryland voter registry on the basis that:

  • the Maryland State Constitution restricted voting to men

  • the Legislature of Maryland had refused to ratify the 19th Amendment

  • "So great an addition to the electorate, if made without the State's consent, destroys its autonomy as a political body."

This last bit is trenchant. Imagine a theoretical Amendment which said that any citizen of the United States could vote in any State's election. If you lived in California, you could send in a ballot by mail and vote for the Governor of Mississippi, or Arkansas, or what-have-you. Of course the population of out-of-state voters would overwhelm the much smaller proportion of in-state voters, and the winner would have no legitimacy as a representative of the State. Such an Amendment would be an attack on State sovereignty and rightly found unconstitutional under the 10th Amendment.

Leser simply argues that the same is true of adding hundreds of thousands of women to the vote against Maryland's will. (A quick check of the U.S. Census shows that in 1910, women outnumbered men in Maryland.)

But the Supreme Court rejected this logic, likening the 19th Amendment to the 15th, which it was modeled upon. If we can make it illegal for you to prohibit blacks from voting, the argument went, we can make it illegal for you to prohibit women from voting.

The question of numbers was never addressed.

The reasoning for such a momentous shift in our electoral destiny was surprisingly facile, but we'd fought a bloody civil war to force the 14th and 15th Amendments on the country, and once that was done, the precedent was set for all sorts of insanity to follow, including the 18th Amendment, bringing us Prohibition, which passed the same year as women got the vote. (Both movements were intimately intertwined.)

There's no Constitutional cause of action in the dilemma you lay out -- one where women vote as a bloc, to the detriment of men. Men aren't dying in electorally significant numbers today, but it's clear from exit polls that women are steering the country on a radically different course than men would choose, and one that is to their and the nation's detriment.

The best course of action, in my opinion, is to repeal and replace the 14th, which is surprisingly doable, and would restore an enormous amount of power back to the States.
